pr_title: Adds Constructor Overload to PeriodCountConsolidatorBase that Accepts PyObject
pr_body:
#### Description
Adds constructor overload to `PeriodCountConsolidatorBase` (and inheritaded classed) that accepts `PyObject`.

#### Related Issue
Closes #3780 #3801 

Thank you, @prasadsom for #3801. Its commits are part of this pull request. I just added unit tests for all consolidators.

#### Motivation and Context
Be able to use the equivalent of `Func<DateTime, CalendarInfo>` func in Python.

#### Requires Documentation Change
Yes. In the consolidator's docs, there is no reference to `Func<DateTime, CalendarInfo>` contructor overload.

#### How Has This Been Tested?
Extends existing unit tests to new `PyObject` overload.

issue_context.title: Adds Constructor Overload to PeriodCountConsolidatorBase that Accepts PyObject
issue_context.body:
#### Expected Behavior
Be able to use the equivalent of `Func<DateTime, CalendarInfo> func` in python.

#### Actual Behavior
Can only use the `Expiry` helper class.

#### Potential Solution
Implement constructor overload that accepts a `PyObject` that represent a `Func<DateTime, CalendarInfo> func`

#### Reproducing the Problem
```python
class ConsolildatorFuncPy(QCAlgorithm):
    def Initialize(self):
        self.SetStartDate(2014, 5, 1)
        self.SetEndDate(2014, 5, 15)
        
        self.AddForex("EURUSD")
        
        x = QuoteBarConsolidator(self.Func)
        x.DataConsolidated += self.OnDataConsolidated
        self.SubscriptionManager.AddConsolidator("EURUSD", x)

    def Func(self, dt):
        period = timedelta(days=1)
        start_time = datetime(dt.year, dt.month, dt.day, 17)
        if start_time > dt:
            start_time = start_time - period
        return CalendarInfo(start_time, period)

    def OnDataConsolidated(self, sender, bar):
        self.Debug(bar.EndTime)
```

- [x] I have confirmed that this is not a duplicate issue by searching [issues](https://github.com/QuantConnect/Lean/issues)
- [x] I have provided detailed steps to reproduce the issue
comments:
Can Python code not use `Func` from .Net `System` namespace ?

Code can be modified with one extra line ,
```
class ConsolildatorFuncPy(QCAlgorithm):
    def Initialize(self):
        self.SetStartDate(2014, 5, 1)
        self.SetEndDate(2014, 5, 15)
        
        self.AddForex("EURUSD")

        #Func here is from .Net System namespace
        func_obj = Func[DateTime,CalendarInfo](self.Func)
        x = QuoteBarConsolidator(func_obj)
        x.DataConsolidated += self.OnDataConsolidated
        self.SubscriptionManager.AddConsolidator("EURUSD", x)

    def Func(self, dt):
        period = timedelta(days=1)
        start_time = datetime(dt.year, dt.month, dt.day, 17)
        if start_time > dt:
            start_time = start_time - period
        return CalendarInfo(start_time, period)

    def OnDataConsolidated(self, sender, bar):
        self.Debug(bar.EndTime)

```

Hi @prasadsom ,
Yes, we can use `System.Func`, but we don't want to ask Python algorithms to include `C#` objects explicitly.

review_comments:
Why add this? It hides the base's property. _Also_ -- typically, if you're going to hide a base class property you should be explicit by using the `new` keyword:

``` csharp
public new TradeBar WorkingBar => (TradeBar)WorkingData;
```

I'm not a fan of this change. If the goal is to provide strongly typed data, then why not do it using generics? `PeriodCountConsolidatorBase<T, TradeBar>` exposes the correct types, so this definition could be pushed all the up (or down depending on how you look at it) the type heirarchy so that _everyone_ gets this behavior instead of just this class _and also_ we won't need to hide properties which can get yucky since behavior becomes dependent on the static (compile-time) type of an object. I've seen some pretty gnarly bugs from such semantics.

Feel free to reach out to discuss further.
The `WorkingBar` was already present, I believe he just refactored into an expression-bodied property, right @AlexCatarino ?
